full_text_en:
Guiding Case No. 240

Qin v. Beijing a Certain Automotive Technology Development Service Co., Ltd. — labor dispute

(Discussed and adopted by the Adjudication Committee of the Supreme People's Court, released on December 20, 2024)

Keywords

Civil; labor dispute; confirmation of labor relationship; new forms of employment; chauffeur driver; necessary operational management; absence of labor relationship

Ruling Gist

Where a platform enterprise or a platform-employment cooperative enterprise carries out necessary operational management to maintain normal platform operation and provide high-quality services, but does not establish dominant labor management, the people's court shall not support, in accordance with the law, the worker's claim that a labor relationship exists between the worker and the enterprise.

Basic Facts

On December 31, 2020, Qin registered an account on the driver-end application of a certain chauffeur platform and applied to become a chauffeur driver. The platform operator was Beijing a Certain Automotive Technology Development Service Co., Ltd. (hereinafter referred to as "Beijing a Certain Automotive Company"). The platform's "Information Service Agreement" stipulated: Beijing a Certain Automotive Company provides paid chauffeur information services to chauffeur drivers; chauffeur drivers accept orders through Beijing a Certain Automotive Company's platform and enter into and perform the "Chauffeur Service Agreement" with users of the chauffeur service; the platform records various information and data during the chauffeur service process; chauffeur drivers collect chauffeur service fees from users of the chauffeur service based on platform data and pay information service fees to Beijing a Certain Automotive Company; Beijing a Certain Automotive Company does not actually provide chauffeur services, nor does it act as an agent for any party on the platform; it merely serves as an intermediary between the chauffeur driver and the user of the chauffeur service to facilitate the conclusion of the "Chauffeur Service Agreement"; Beijing a Certain Automotive Company has no labor, service, employment, or any similar relationship with the chauffeur driver, but is entitled to supervise the chauffeur driver's service activities and fee collection in accordance with platform rules, and is entitled to evaluate the chauffeur driver's service activities based on platform user feedback, and to conduct corresponding investigations and dispositions.

In the actual performance of the agreement, Beijing a Certain Automotive Company did not manage Qin as an employee, nor did it require him to comply with the company's labor rules and regulations. After a user of the chauffeur service sent out a request for chauffeur service, the platform uniformly dispatched orders to eligible drivers, and Qin decided on his own whether to accept or grab orders. Qin only needed to purchase a uniform, undergo software usage training, take a road test, and accept random appearance inspections; he had a high degree of autonomy in terms of working hours and workload, and could freely decide whether to register to use the platform, when to use the platform to engage in chauffeur services, etc. The remuneration Qin received for engaging in chauffeur services was the chauffeur service fee, which was paid directly by the user of the chauffeur service.

In addition, the platform adopted reward and penalty measures such as awarding or deducting gold coins based on the chauffeur driver's order acceptance rate. Gold coins awarded by the platform could be used by the chauffeur driver to purchase platform "props" to increase the success rate of subsequent order grabbing, and were not directly related to his income. The platform collected data such as the number of completed orders and the rate of cancellations attributable to the driver, and implemented account suspension and other risk control measures on chauffeur driver accounts with significantly abnormal order-taking conditions.

Subsequently, a labor dispute arose between the parties. Qin applied for labor arbitration, requesting Beijing a Certain Automotive Company to pay the difference of twice the wages for failure to conclude a written labor contract for the period from January 31, 2021 to January 31, 2022, in the amount of RMB 8,074.38. The Labor and Personnel Dispute Arbitration Committee of Shijingshan District, Beijing, ruled: reject Qin's arbitration request. Dissatisfied, Qin filed a lawsuit with the Shijingshan District People's Court of Beijing.

Judgment

The Shijingshan District People's Court of Beijing rendered a civil judgment on March 31, 2023 (No. (2023) Jing 0107 Min Chu 2196): reject all of Qin's claims. After the judgment was pronounced, Qin disagreed and appealed. The Beijing No. 1 Intermediate People's Court rendered a civil judgment on September 15, 2023 (No. (2023) Jing 01 Min Zhong 6036): reject the appeal and affirm the original judgment.

Reasoning

The disputed issue in this case is: whether a labor relationship exists between the platform operator, Beijing a Certain Automotive Company, and the chauffeur driver, Qin.

The essential characteristic of a labor relationship is dominant labor management, i.e., a strong degree of personal subordination, economic subordination, and organizational subordination between the worker and the employer. Under new forms of employment, in determining whether labor management exists, the focus should still be on examining and accurately determining whether the enterprise exercises dominant labor management over the worker and whether the labor provided by the worker has the characteristics of subordination.

In this case, although Beijing a Certain Automotive Company exercised a certain degree of operational management over the chauffeur driver Qin in accordance with the agreement, such management did not constitute dominant labor management; Qin had the right to independently decide whether to register to use the platform, when to use the platform, whether to accept or grab orders, and had no strong subordination to Beijing a Certain Automotive Company. Specifically: First, in terms of the content of the relevant agreements, Beijing a Certain Automotive Company provides paid chauffeur information services to chauffeur drivers; chauffeur drivers accept orders through Beijing a Certain Automotive Company's platform and enter into transactions with users of the chauffeur service; chauffeur drivers collect chauffeur service fees from users of the chauffeur service in accordance with the agreement and pay information service fees to Beijing a Certain Automotive Company; Beijing a Certain Automotive Company does not actually provide chauffeur services, nor does it act as an agent for any party on the platform; it merely serves as an intermediary between the chauffeur driver and the user of the chauffeur service; chauffeur drivers are free to decide whether to use the platform to receive information services. Second, in terms of the actual performance of the agreement, Qin had the right to independently decide his working hours and location, rather than accepting orders according to Beijing a Certain Automotive Company's work arrangements; moreover, Beijing a Certain Automotive Company did not manage Qin as an employee in terms of commuting time, attendance, etc., so there was no subordinate relationship of management and being managed between the parties. Qin's income was withdrawn from his platform account; the funds withdrawn originated from the user of the chauffeur service and were paid directly by the user of the chauffeur service to Qin's account on the platform, after which Qin applied to the platform for withdrawal; the timing of withdrawal was determined by Qin himself, and the remuneration was not paid by Beijing a Certain Automotive Company. Third, although Beijing a Certain Automotive Company required Qin to purchase a uniform, undergo software usage training, take a road test, and accept random appearance inspections, and awarded or deducted gold coins based on Qin's order acceptance rate, these measures constituted necessary operational management to maintain normal platform operation and provide high-quality services; Beijing a Certain Automotive Company's measures such as account suspension based on data such as Qin's number of completed orders and rate of cancellations attributable to the driver, and abnormal order-taking conditions, were also necessary operational measures taken based on reasonable risk control.

In conclusion, the work requirements imposed by Beijing a Certain Automotive Company on the chauffeur driver Qin were necessary operational management measures taken to maintain normal platform operation and provide high-quality services, and did not constitute dominant labor management. Accordingly, it should not be determined in accordance with the law that a labor relationship exists between the parties.

Relevant Legal Provisions

Article 7 of the Labor Contract Law of the People's Republic of China

Article 90 of the Interpretation of the Supreme People's Court on the Application of the Civil Procedure Law of the People's Republic of China (Fa Shi [2015] No. 5, amended in 2022)
